description: Finalist B desk track: four research tracks, verifier results, completeness critic. Copied from the workflow journal; agent results in journal order.

findings.claim: Chiang Mai 2018 study: four Thai soy-milk brands, two flavours each, total isoflavones 25.5 to 63.5 mg per 250 ml serving, with marked variation between lots of the same product.
findings.note: Hirattanapun E, Teekachunhatean S. J Health Sci Med Res 2018;36(2):117-26, published 2018-05-24. Read from the journal's own page and abstract, not the full PDF. The authors state that standardising or declaring isoflavone content is needed. Not on the page: brand names, per-lot values, per-100 mL values, lot count.

findings.claim: EFSA press release, 21 Oct 2015 (Isoflavones in food supplements for post-menopausal women: no evidence of harm): no indication of harm at isoflavone levels typical of food supplements, limited to the doses and durations studied (3 months to just under 1 year); no data for women in transition to menopause or with a personal or family history of cancer.
findings.note: This is the EFSA press release, not the scientific opinion. It gives no mg/day doses and no tolerable upper intake level or safe-maximum statement. It cites DOI 10.2903/j.efsa.2015.4246.

findings.claim: EFSA 2015 full scientific opinion (DOI 10.2903/j.efsa.2015.4246): doses studied in mg/day, any UL or safe-dose statement, and excluded populations.
findings.note: Full opinion not reachable with the tools used. Only the press release was read. Title per search results: 'Risk assessment for peri- and post-menopausal women taking food supplements containing isolated isoflavones' (EFSA Journal 13(10):4246).

findings.claim: EFSA 2015 set no tolerable upper intake level and no safe maximum daily intake for isoflavone supplements.
findings.note: Secondary only. The snippet says EFSA could not set a single health-based guidance value or safe intake level for isoflavone supplements as a group. It also reports endometrial hyperplasia in 6 of 154 women taking 150 mg/day for 5 years, which EFSA did not treat as adverse. Confirm against the primary opinion. The press release is silent on a UL.

findings.claim: Mahidol Faculty of Pharmacy knowledge sheet lists 9.65 for 'Soy milk, fluid' in an isoflavone table.
findings.source: https://pharmacy.mahidol.ac.th/knowledge/files/0002.pdf (saved copy, text decoded from its content streams)
findings.note: The row label and value are present in the decoded text. The table heading reads 'Isoflavones' with columns for phytoestrogen, daidzein, genistein and glycitein; the column assignment is inferred from layout. The sheet is undated: PDF metadata CreateDate 2010-02-03, not an issue date. Academic, not legal.

findings.claim: The Mahidol value 9.65 is mg per 100 g of plain soy milk.
findings.note: The unit header is in Thai glyphs that could not be decoded. The value could be per 100 g or per 100 mL. Arithmetic only: 9.65 x 2.5 = 24.1 mg per 250 ml, just below the 2018 minimum of 25.5 mg. Not used in the screen.

findings.claim: Mahidol intake guide: 50 to 100 mg isoflavones per day, roughly 2 to 4 glasses of soy milk.
findings.note: The tokens '50-100', '2 - 4' and '100' are present in the PDF text, but the sentence linking them to a daily intake is not decodable. Academic guidance, not a legal limit, undated, non-binding.

findings.claim: Prior desk check cites EFSA pub/2847 for EFSA rejecting a soy-isoflavone menopause claim (DOI 10.2903/j.efsa.2012.2847).
findings.note: The snippet describes 2847 as an opinion on health claims for soy isoflavones and bone density and menopausal vasomotor symptoms. It is not the 2015 opinion. The 'rejected' wording rests on a trade-press summary. Check the primary text before the entry cites it.

findings.claim: Screen result: no labelled total in the grid (added extract 10 to 50 mg; labels 40 to 100 mg per serving) keeps 90 percent or more of servings within plus or minus 15 percent of the label. Best cell: 73.4 percent (50 mg extract, 100 mg label).
findings.note: Computed, not a source fact. Closed-form exact probability; a seeded Monte Carlo (seed 20261018, n=200,000) agrees within 0.0034. ASSUMPTIONS: base uniform on 25.5 to 63.5 mg; extract within +/-10 percent, uniform, independent per serving (unsourced).

findings.claim: Base-spread requirement for 90 percent in-window (nominal label = 44.5 mg base midpoint + added dose): full base width 18.2 to 29.2 mg for 10 to 50 mg extract, against 38 mg in the 2018 range. At 30 mg extract (nominal 74.5 mg), base must stay roughly 32.5 to 56.5 mg per 250 ml.
findings.note: Computed. ASSUMPTIONS: nominal label equals base midpoint plus added dose; 90 percent target; uniform base.

findings.claim: Without base control, 90 percent of servings fall within plus or minus 15 percent only at an added extract near 90 mg (nominal total about 135 mg). Shares at the nominal label: 0.8536 at 70 mg, 0.8860 at 80 mg, 0.9105 at 90 mg.
findings.source: D:\Workspace\singha-case-study\rework\screen\soy_isoflavone_dose_screen.py run with --added-mg 60 70 80 90 100 120 (output to scratch, not saved in the repo)
findings.note: Computed under the same assumptions. A dose this large is far above the 50 to 100 mg per day guide and is not a practical route. The extract's own tolerance then dominates the variance.

findings.claim: A single fixed plus or minus 15 percent window that contains every serving needs about 246.5 mg of added extract.
findings.note: Closed-form arithmetic under the stated assumptions. Shows that a fixed label cannot be met for every serving at any practical dose unless base soy is controlled.

findings.claim: Floor label 'at least 50 mg' per serving needs 27.2 mg added extract under worst case (base 25.5 mg, extract at minus 10 percent). At 30 mg, worst case is 52.5 mg, or 51.1 mg with the Mahidol-scaled 24.1 mg base.
findings.note: Computed under the 2018 range assumption. The upper end is not controlled by a floor: at 30 mg extract the serving range is about 52.5 to 96.5 mg.

findings.claim: Sourcing implication: base soy must be standardised or lot-tested before any plus or minus 15 percent total can be labelled. Lot-specific dosing (measure base per lot, then set extract per lot) is a possible route.
findings.source: Inference from the 2018 lot variation (https://he01.tci-thaijo.org/index.php/jhsmr/article/view/125491) and the screen results above
findings.note: This is the screen's reading, not a tested result. Lot-specific dosing is untested. Measurement error of the lot assay is not modelled.

findings.claim: Recommended labelled claim: 'at least 50 mg' total isoflavones per 250 ml serving, with about 30 mg standardised extract, conditional on lot-tested base soy. No point label with plus or minus 15 percent.
findings.note: Conditional on the base lot minimum being at least about 25 mg and the extract certificate of analysis holding within 10 percent. No health benefit is claimed. Safety for women aged 40 to 59 is not settled by this screen.

open_items: Full EFSA 2015 opinion (DOI 10.2903/j.efsa.2015.4246): needed for the doses studied in mg/day, any UL or safe-dose statement, and excluded populations. Wiley returned HTTP 403; access needs an institutional or library copy.
Unit of the Mahidol 9.65 value (per 100 g or per 100 mL): get the Thai-language sheet text, a second composition table, or a lab assay of the team's own plain soy milk.
Full PDF of the Chiang Mai 2018 article: brand-level values, lot count, and whether any brand declares isoflavone content. The PDF is linked from the journal page.
Plain unsweetened UHT base: the 2018 products were two flavours per brand, so plain base isoflavone content is unmeasured. Needs the team's own lot-level assay of plain base soy.
Certificate of analysis for a standardised isoflavone extract: the plus or minus 10 percent tolerance is an assumption, and no supplier was verified.

Safety of a 50 to 100 mg per day total in women aged 40 to 59, including perimenopausal women and women with a cancer history. EFSA gives no data for these groups. Needs a regulatory or medical review; this screen makes no safety conclusion.
Thai FDA route for a total-isoflavone declaration on a food: not checked in this track. The prior desk check's claim-route finding (Notification 447) was not re-checked here.
Prior desk check's EFSA pub/2847 citation: check the primary text before use (see the finding on pub/2847).
Prior-check items not re-checked here: the 2005 Japanese panel figures (secondary, nutraingredients) and the absence of any Thai isoflavone intake limit.
results.verdict: Dose track result for finalist B. (a) The 2018 Chiang Mai range of 25.5 to 63.5 mg per 250 ml is verified from the journal article page, with lot variation confirmed; the authors call for standardising or declaring isoflavone content. (b) The EFSA 2015 press release is verified: no harm at supplement-level doses over 3 months to just under a year, and no data for women in transition to menopause or with a cancer history. The full opinion was unreachable (HTTP 403), so the UL and dose-list statements stay unverified. (c) Mahidol lists 9.65 for soy milk in its isoflavone table, but the unit (per 100 g or per 100 mL) is unverified; the 50 to 100 mg per day guide is academic, undated and non-binding. (d) Screen at D:\Workspace\singha-case-study\rework\screen\soy_isoflavone_dose_screen.py, results in soy_isoflavone_dose_screen_results.json in the same folder. With the 2018 base range and plus or minus 10 percent extract tolerance, no label in the 40 to 100 mg grid keeps 90 percent of servings within plus or minus 15 percent; the best is 73 percent. Recommended claim: 'at least 50 mg' total isoflavones per 250 ml, with about 30 mg standardised extract, conditional on lot testing of the base soy. This implies base soy must be standardised or lot-tested. A plus or minus 15 percent point label needs base held to about 32.5 to 56.5 mg at 30 mg extract. No health benefit is claimed.

results.reason: The claim holds against the cited source. The results JSON states all 35 grid cells (added extract 10 to 50 mg, labels 40 to 100 mg). The highest exact share is 0.7339 at 50 mg extract and 100 mg label, which rounds to 73.4 percent, and no cell reaches 0.90. None of the three refutation conditions applies: the source states the claim, the base range comes from the 2018 article's own abstract rather than a secondary report (the JSON notes only the full PDF was not read), and the run date 2026-10-18 is today. Caveats the claim does not disclose: the 90 percent threshold is the script's TARGET_SHARE, flagged ASSUMPTION and not sourced; the shares depend on flagged assumptions (uniform base distribution across 25.5 to 63.5 mg, uniform plus or minus 10 percent certificate-of-analysis tolerance, independence); the 73.4 figure is the exact method, while Monte Carlo gives 73.5 percent.

results.reason: The source states the claim's substance. The study sampled two flavours of each of four soy-milk brands from retail outlets in Chiang Mai, reports total isoflavones of 25.5 to 63.5 mg per 250 mL serving, and reports marked variation among lots of the same product. It is a primary original article published in 2018, so it is neither a secondary report nor out of date for describing what that study found. Two wording points are not refutation grounds: the source says the products were commercially available in Thailand, not that the brands are Thai-made, and it gives no sampling dates, so "2018" refers to the publication year. The number of lots tested is not stated, and the claim does not assert it.
results.evidence:
1. WebFetch of https://he01.tci-thaijo.org/index.php/jhsmr/article/view/125491 returned a summarizing-model answer. I did not rely on its quotations.
2. I downloaded the raw landing page with curl to D:\Temp/jhsmr_125491.html and grepped the raw HTML. The abstract text there confirms: "Two flavors of each of 4 brands of soy milk were obtained from retail outlets in Chiang Mai, Thailand." Genistin and daidzin were the main isoflavones, measured by HPLC. Total isoflavones were "ranging from 25.5 to 63.5 mg per serving (250 mL) of soy milk." "Marked variation in total isoflavones was also found even among different lots of the same product." The conclusion calls for standardizing or declaring isoflavone content.
3. Raw HTML confirms the DOI as https://doi.org/10.31584/jhsmr.2018.36.2.5 and the Chiang Mai University (Faculty of Medicine, Department of Pharmacology) affiliations.
4. Title ("Variability of Isoflavone Content in Soy Milk Products Commercially Available in Thailand"), authors, journal (JHSMR), Vol. 36 No. 2 (2018), page range and the 2018-05-24 publication date came from the WebFetch summary. I did not independently re-verify these in the raw HTML beyond the DOI.
5. Searches of the raw HTML for sample-collection or purchase dates returned nothing, so the sampling period is unstated.
6. The source describes "soy milk products commercially available in Thailand." It does not state brand origin, so "Thai soy-milk brands" is an inference, not a quoted fact.

findings.claim: Chulalongkorn menopause clinic, 2025 (Sirisivanart et al., J Psychiatr Assoc Thai 70(2):297-305): 102 women aged 45-60; insomnia prevalence 52% (ISI >= 8); anxiety associated with insomnia (OR 12.57, 95% CI 1.56-101.50).
findings.note: Single tertiary-hospital menopause clinic, cross-sectional. Hot-flush and night-sweat prevalence not reported on the page. Clinic sample, so not a community rate.

findings.claim: Multicentre Thai cohort (Asian Biomedicine 2017, 11(3):207-216, Siriraj; corresponding author Wongwananuruk): 870 peri- and postmenopausal women (mean age 51.8 +/- 5.6) at 9 menopause clinics in 4 regions. The three most common symptoms were psychoemotional distress, musculoskeletal pain and hot flushes.
findings.note: Abstract only. No hot-flush, night-sweat or sleep percentage on the page. Clinic-based sample. Full text not read.

findings.claim: Two-city Thai study (Sriprasert et al., Climacteric, April 2017): 632 women (320 Bangkok, 312 Chiang Mai), mean age 50.9. Hot flushes or night sweats prevalence 65%; mean 8.7 episodes per week; problem rating 4.3/10. Chiang Mai women rated the symptoms as more problematic, but prevalence and frequency were similar.
findings.note: Read only as a search excerpt; the journal page was not opened. Volume 20(2) and pages 171-177 are not confirmed (the USC Keck faculty page, https://keck.usc.edu/faculty-search/intira-sriprasert/, lists the 2017 Climacteric title only). Recruitment and sampling not stated. Largest Thai figure found, but not known to be community-based.

findings.claim: Hospital-based survey, Songklanagarind Hospital, southern Thailand (PubMed 16428122, 2006): 270 women aged 45-65; hot flushes 36.8%, night sweats 20.8%, vaginal dryness 55.3% (MENQOL instrument).
findings.note: The PubMed page returned only a cookie notice. Figures come from two search excerpts that agree. Hospital-based, so likely to overstate community rates.

findings.claim: Older Thai samples (1997): (i) 119 postmenopausal women in the Klong Toey slum, randomly selected by home number; vasomotor symptoms 72.3%, and 29.4% of them rated severe vasomotor symptoms as a problem. (ii) 268 women aged 40-59 accompanying patients to a Bangkok hospital outpatient department; insomnia and hot flushes among the symptoms most associated with menopausal status (P<0.001).
findings.source: WebSearch excerpts from this run, query 'prevalence menopausal symptoms community-based Thai women general population survey sleep quality hot flushes Thailand'; no page opened
findings.note: Both are 1997 studies. The Klong Toey sample is the only community-style estimate found, and it is low-income and old. The second sample is outpatient companions, not a community sample.

findings.claim: No Thai community or general-population estimate of night sweats or sleep disturbance among women aged 40-59 was found. The only Thai sleep prevalence found is clinic-based (Chulalongkorn, 52%).
findings.source: WebSearch results from this run (English and Thai queries on Thai menopausal symptom prevalence, sleep and community samples); no single page
findings.note: This is an absence search, so it is not proof of absence. The searches did not return any Thai community study using PSQI, ISI or a similar validated sleep measure. National survey data (NSO) not found.

findings.claim: Mintel 'Thailand Women's Wellness Consumer Report 2026': public page shows the title, a timestamp of 30 June 2026 (not labelled as a publication date), price USD 2,995 excl. tax, and headlines 'Sleep is Thailand's white space for women's wellness innovation' and 'Gen X women have the lowest self-perceived overall wellbeing'. The key opportunity named is hormone regulation. Menopause, hot flushes, soy and isoflavone do not appear on the public page. The full report is paywalled.
findings.note: Public summary only. No figures visible. The 'Key takeaways' body is not visible.

findings.claim: File claim (rework/01 section B, Fit score 2): the midlife reason 'is tied to a Mintel Thailand women's wellness report (June 2026)'.
findings.note: Partly supported. The public Mintel page supports a sleep angle and a Gen X wellbeing gap. It does not name menopause, hot flushes or midlife women, and the full report was not readable. The menopause link rests on no visible Mintel text.

findings.claim: Kasetsart University survey (Tipkanon et al., Kasetsart J Soc Sci 32(3):493-502, published 31 Dec 2011): 402 women aged 40-59 (menopausal). 85.8% had consumed pasteurised or UHT soymilk (the most commonly consumed soy product). 87.6% were interested in soy germ products containing isoflavones. Preferred development as a beverage 57.7%; as a supplementary food 25.3%. 87.1% usually buy from markets or open markets.
findings.note: Abstract page only; the PDF was not read. Stated interest, not purchase. Sampling method and questionnaire not on the abstract page. The isoflavone product tested was soy germ, not soy milk. Capsules are not mentioned in the abstract. This is the only Thai survey of this age group on soy or isoflavone products found.

findings.claim: File claim (rework/01 section B, target line): the group 'prefer[s] a daily food to capsules'.
findings.note: No source found for food-versus-capsule preference in women aged 40-59. The only form data are the Kasetsart beverage (57.7%) and supplementary food (25.3%) figures, with no capsule option in the abstract.

findings.claim: Supplement use among health-conscious pre- and post-menopausal Thai women (Leerasiri et al., J Med Assoc Thai 93(10):1128-1136, 2010): 327 women aged 40-67 who joined a health-promotion programme at Siriraj Menopause Clinic, Jan-Jul 2008. 54.7% took at least one supplement (37.3% current, 17.4% past users). No soy-drink or product-form data in the excerpt.
findings.note: Search excerpt only. The repository page returned only a DSpace label on WebFetch. Clinic-based, 2008 data, and not form-specific in the excerpt.

findings.claim: Khon Kaen Municipality survey (Sangsunanon and Phanomai, J Health Syst Res Dev 16(1):57-71, 2023): 206 adults aged 20-59, 68.9% female. Most bought health-maintenance supplements. Attitude associated with consumption (OR 6.19, 95% CI 2.48-15.44). No age split and no product-form data.
findings.note: Abstract page only. Sampling method not stated. Not restricted to women aged 40-59 and not about soy or isoflavone products.

findings.claim: European survey (Koebnick et al., Climacteric 8(3):230-242, 2005; DOI 10.1080/13697130500118092): 465 postmenopausal women in Germany, Denmark, Italy and the UK. Declared acceptability of isoflavones was 80% (Germany), 75% (Italy), 59% (UK), 55% (Denmark). Preferred product forms differed markedly between countries; the forms are not named in the abstract.
findings.note: Non-Thai comparator only. Abstract page. Ages not reported on the page.

findings.claim: Mintel 'Milk and Dairy Alternatives, Thai Consumer, 2022': cow and soy milk have the highest penetration in Thailand, and digestibility concerns keep consumers aged 45 and over off cow's milk.
findings.source: https://clients.mintel.com/download/brochure/milk-and-dairy-alternatives-thai-consumer-2022 (WebFetch returned bookmarks only); WebSearch excerpt from this run
findings.note: The PDF text could not be read, so no figures were seen. Access terms unknown; looks like a commercial excerpt.

findings.claim: Mintel 'Thailand Functional Food and Drink Market Report 2026' public page: price USD 2,995 excl. tax; no visible figures. The public text does not mention hormones, menopause, hot flushes, sleep, soy or isoflavone. Only a contents item 'make at-home sweet snacking work harder for women's health goals' refers to women. Paywalled.
findings.note: Public page only.

findings.claim: A Mintel 2025 functional food report calls for life-stage products for women tied to perceived hormonal symptoms, and its primary targets are younger Millennials and Gen X.
findings.source: WebSearch excerpt from this run; the 2025 report was not opened
findings.note: The 2026 public page does not repeat the life-stage claim. Treat as unverified until the 2025 public page or summary is read.

findings.claim: Willingness to pay for soy milk among Muslim farming households in southern Thailand (Thaiburi et al., Journal of Economics Maejo University 5(1), Jan-Jun 2025): 400 parents of children aged 6-14 in 13 districts of Narathiwat, sampled purposively and accidentally in community stores, flea markets and convenience stores (Sep-Oct 2022). Double-bounded contingent valuation for 300 ml soy milk against 300 ml cow's milk, with starting prices of 2-5 baht. Estimated WTP premium 3.15 baht per 300 ml. Significant factors: number of children, education, household income, price and marketing communication.
findings.note: The PDF's first-page abstract describes a Khon Kaen tourism study, not soy milk, so the abstract on file does not match the title. The sample is low-income households with children, not women aged 40-59. The comparator is cow's milk. The product is plain soy milk, not functional. The prices are far below any plausible retail price for a 250 ml functional drink.

findings.claim: Willingness to use functional drinks in Bangkok (Prasertsakul and Worawitphinyo, Executive Journal 40(2):51-63, Dec 2020): 403 respondents at major public areas in Bangkok. Attitude, perceived health claims and credibility of the information source significantly affected willingness to use. Health concern had no significant effect.
findings.note: No price, WTP or percentage figures in the abstract. Not soy-specific and not about menopause.

findings.claim: Marketbuzzz survey (reported by Brand Buffet, 5 Sep 2024): 500 Thai respondents, July 2024. 70% would pay more for organic products, mostly 10-20% (37% named that band; about 4% up to 30%). Price (56%) and taste (40%) were among the top factors in food purchase.
findings.note: Secondary news report; the underlying survey was not opened. Food only, not drinks or soy. Age range not reported.

findings.claim: No Thai study measuring willingness to pay for a functional soy drink or an isoflavone soy drink was found.
findings.source: WebSearch queries from this run (English and Thai, about 5 queries, including 'ยินดีจ่ายเพิ่ม เครื่องดื่มเพื่อสุขภาพ ผลิตภัณฑ์นมถั่วเหลือง'); no single page
findings.note: Absence search. Closest findings are the Maejo 2025, Bangkok functional drinks and Marketbuzzz items above. The Mahidol IPSR and MDPI items below could not be read.

findings.claim: Mahidol IPSR survey on sugary drinks and healthier-choice labels (2023-24 project PDF) includes average drink spending and may include WTP for healthier drinks.
findings.note: Not read. The likeliest Thai source for drink spending, but no figures seen and soy milk coverage unknown.

findings.claim: MDPI Sustainability 14(19):11957 (2022), 'Consumers' Intention to Purchase Functional Non-Dairy Milk and Gender-Based Market Segmentation': the title suggests a gender-based purchase-intent study of functional non-dairy milk.
findings.note: Not read. Country, sample, age and WTP unknown. Do not use as Thai evidence until checked.

findings.claim: Test spec in rework/01 section B: spike plain soy milk with a standardised isoflavone powder at two doses; then a blind taste and purchase-intent test with 30 Thai women aged 40-59; check the powder's certificate of analysis; gate: the dose range needs a safety review before any consumer tasting. The target is defined by age only.
findings.note: Read from the file.

findings.claim: The 30-woman test as specified has no price or willingness-to-pay element and no screen for hot flushes, night sweats or disturbed sleep.
findings.source: D:\Workspace\singha-case-study\rework\01_ideas_from_zero.md (section B, First test and Target); D:\Workspace\singha-case-study\rework\02_desk_kill_tests.md (section B, kill test and 'Not settled')
findings.note: Reading of the spec text. Because the reason to buy is hot flushes or sleep, an unscreened sample cannot show whether the symptomatic target would buy.

findings.claim: At n=30, Wilson 95% intervals: 0/30 gives upper bound 11%; 10/30 gives 19-51%; 15/30 gives 33-67%; 20/30 gives 49-81%. A 50/50 margin of error is about +/-18 points. For a paired two-dose preference, a two-sided exact sign test reaches p<0.05 only at 21/30 (70%) or more in one direction (p=0.043); 20/30 gives p=0.099.
findings.source: Computed in this run (Python, Wilson score interval and exact binomial test)
findings.note: Arithmetic check. Assumes simple random sampling and a within-woman paired design; a between-group design would be weaker.

findings.claim: Chiang Mai study of commercial Thai soy milk (Hirattanapun and Teekachunhatean, J Health Sci Med Res 36(2):117-26, 2018): 8 products (two flavours from each of four brands) bought at Chiang Mai retail. Isoflavones 25.5-63.5 mg per 250 ml serving, with marked variation between lots of the same product. The authors call for standardising or declaring isoflavone content. The study does not say whether products were plain or flavoured.
findings.note: Conflicts with the file's premise that 'plain Thai soy milk carries little isoflavone naturally' (rework/01 section B, Feasibility line). Plain-product question is still open. Two servings would supply about 51-127 mg (arithmetic). The desk check (rework/02 section B, check 4) reported the same range but did not flag the conflict.

open_items: No Thai national or community prevalence estimate for hot flushes, night sweats or sleep disturbance in women aged 40-59 was found. Next: NSO or Thai Health Examination Survey menopause items, or a community study using PSQI or ISI.
Full text of Kasetsart 2011 (sampling, questionnaire, purchase and product-form items, whether capsules were offered). The abstract alone cannot support purchase or form preference.
Full text or journal record of Sriprasert 2017 (recruitment, volume and pages) and Songklanagarind 2006 (PubMed page not opened).
Full text of Leerasiri 2010 (form-specific data; the sample is from 2008 at a single clinic).

Mintel full reports are paywalled at USD 2,995 each (Women's Wellness 2026, Functional Food and Drink 2026). Menopause, soy and isoflavone coverage is unknown. The 2022 milk-alternatives brochure text was not readable.

Maejo 2025 WTP: the paper's abstract on file does not match its title, and the sample is low-income parents of children aged 6-14 in Narathiwat with a cow's milk comparator. Confirm with the authors or a clean copy before any use.

Mahidol IPSR sugary-drink survey (drink spending and healthier-choice labels) and MDPI 2022 functional non-dairy milk study: neither could be read (HTTP 403). Possibly the best Thai drink-spend and WTP sources.

Whether plain, unsweetened Thai soy milks contain the same isoflavone range as the 2018 Chiang Mai sample (8 products, plain-versus-flavoured not stated). This decides whether the labelled dose is a real point of difference or only a standardisation claim.
No Thai retail price data for a 250 ml functional or isoflavone soy drink. The Maejo starting prices (2-5 baht per 300 ml) should not be used as a price anchor.
No scanner or store data on soy-drink purchase by women aged 40-59. Stated interest (Kasetsart) is not purchase.
The Mintel 2025 functional report's life-stage claim is unverified (search excerpt only).
The file's 'prefer a daily food to capsules' and the Mintel-tied midlife reason have no visible source. Both need either a source or a rewording before the entry.
results.verdict:
Demand case: weak to moderate, and not yet shown for purchase. Thai symptom data exist but come from clinic or two-city samples, not community surveys: 52% insomnia in a 102-woman Bangkok clinic sample (verified), hot flushes among the three most common complaints in an 870-woman nine-clinic cohort (verified), and 65% hot flushes or night sweats in a 632-woman two-city sample (unverified, excerpt only). The labelled dose must reflect total isoflavones and needs a certificate of analysis and lot testing. results.verdict:
Route (a): on the primary text the drink is most likely a conventional food, not a food supplement. The 293 cl. 2 definition requires a form that is not a conventional food form, and a 250 ml UHT drink is one. The purpose element ('consumers expecting health-promotion benefits') is not form-based, and FDA's own 2026 slides say the boundary turns on the purpose stated to consumers. A labelled isoflavone dose plus any menopause or sleep message is the main reclassification risk. The desk's 'pass' should read 'pass on form; open on purpose'.

Registration (b): every food needs a 13-digit food serial number. The operative soy-milk standard is MoPH Notification 198 (B.E. 2543), not a TISI standard. It requires UHT at least 133 C for at least 1 second with aseptic packing, soy protein at least 2 percent and soy fat at least 1 percent. The desk missed it. Two questions are open: whether an isoflavone-fortified drink stays under 198 (cl. 3), and whether the extract triggers the new-food route (FDA slides 9-10, which require a label plus an FDA approval letter). The desk's serial-number basis, 293 cl. 12, is repealed by Notification 411.

Claims (c): no annex of 447 lists a soy, isoflavone, menopause, hot-flush or sleep claim. Such a claim would need an FDA-designated assessment and FDA permission (cl. 5), human intervention evidence in the target group (cl. 2(3)), no implication of relief or treatment of disease (cl. 6(2)), and the 'no effect on treating, relieving, curing or preventing disease' disclaimer (cl. 6(3)(ช)). Hot flushes and sleep are symptoms, which fit poorly under the Thai definition of other-function claims (normal body function). Whether they are 'disease' for cl. 6(2) is not settled by the text. A declared isoflavone dose may itself be a health claim under the broad cl. 1 definition.

Dose (d): no Thai isoflavone limit was found. EFSA (2015) set no upper limit and excluded transition-stage women and women with cancer history. The Chiang Mai study shows plain Thai soy milk already holds 25.5 to 63.5 mg per 250 ml, so the labelled dose must count base-soy isoflavones. The desk's note that plain soy milk carries little isoflavone is contradicted.

Standard (e): TISI applicability is not established. Notification 198 is the mandatory food standard found. Its status as consolidated text is unverified.

Kill test (rework/02 section B): not formally triggered on the primary text, because a cl. 5 approval route exists and the disease question is open. For planning it should be treated as triggered: no annex lists a menopause-linked benefit, the only route needs FDA permission after a recognised assessment, and cl. 6(2) plus the required disclaimer both cut against a relief benefit. Record it as 'provisionally triggered, pending FDA's written reply'.

Written confirmation needed from FDA, or from a registration adviser who will put these to FDA: (1) food or supplement classification, with and without a dose label or sleep or menopause message; (2) whether hot flushes or sleep disturbance count as 'disease' under cl. 6(2), and whether any cl. 5 claim is obtainable; (3) whether a declared isoflavone dose is a health claim; (4) the food serial route, and whether the extract is a novel food; (5) whether an isoflavone-fortified drink stays under Notification 198; (6) the current text of the supplement series (293 with 309, 405, 411, 448), which was not read.

Limits: Thai texts of 293 (pp.1-4), 447 (gazette pp.29-33) and 198 (pp.1-3) were read as page images. FDA slides are official presentations, not legal text. The English 447 is an unofficial FDA translation and is used only where the Thai was not read (Annexes 1 to 3). Notification 448, 411 and 405 texts, the Food Act, and the EFSA 2012 opinion were not read.
